citations.quote: A topological space is **Polish** when it is separable ([[def-separable-space]]) and completely metrizable: its topology is induced by some complete metric ([[lem-complete-remetrisation]]). No particular compatible complete metric or countable dense subset is part of the structure.

A topological space $X$ is **separable** if some at most countable subset $D\subseteq X$ is dense in $X$ ([[def-dense-top]], [[def-countable]]). Equivalently, every nonempty open subset of $X$ meets $D$.

1. $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$ with the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]) is a complete metric space
   ([[def-complete-metric-space]]).
2. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on
   $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ is complete.

**The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited and is not decoration.**
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] defines $\mathbb{R}^n$ and its three metrics only for
$n \ge 1$, because at $n = 0$ the metric $d_\infty$ would be a maximum over the
empty index set. Every statement about $\mathbb{R}^n$ in this library carries the
hypothesis, and this one does too.

$\mathbb{Q} \approx \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]): the rationals are
countably infinite ([[def-countable]]).

**No choice principle is used.** The one place where a reader expects a choice,
"pick a representative $a/b$ of each rational", is exactly where
[[lem-rat-positive-denominator]] applies: every rational *has* a representative
with positive denominator, so the map $(a,b) \mapsto [(a,b)]$ defined on
$\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ is already **surjective** onto $\mathbb{Q}$,
and countability follows from a surjection without ever selecting a
representative. The same device handles $\mathbb{Z}$, which is a surjective image
of $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ by construction ([[def-integers]]).

The map $q \mapsto \hat q$ ([[def-real-numbers]]) is an embedding of ordered
fields. Every real is approximated by rationals: for $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and
rational $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $q \in \mathbb{Q}$ with
$|x - \hat q| < \hat\varepsilon$. Consequently, strictly between any two
reals lies a rational.

A measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$ is **standard Borel** if there are a Polish space $P$ and a bijection $h:E\to P$ such that $A\in\mathcal E$ exactly when $h[A]$ is Borel in $P$. Thus the measurable structure is part of the datum; no particular compatible Polish topology on $E$ is selected.

derivations.claim: By [F4] and [F5], $\mathbb Q$ is a countable dense subset of $\mathbb R$, so [F2] makes the usual real line separable. Its usual metric is complete by [F3]. Thus the usual topology is Polish by [F1].
The identity map from $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$ to the usual Polish real line is a bijection and preserves exactly the Borel sets. The standard-Borel definition [F6] therefore applies.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be non-negative. Then there exists a unique non-negative operator
$R:V\to V$ such that

$$R^2=T.$$

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Assume AC. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then $$\Phi_X(t):=\mathbb E e^{it\cdot X}=\exp(it\cdot m-t^T\Sigma t/2)\qquad(t\in\mathbb R^d).$$ This transform uniquely determines the law, including singular Sigma.

Let $(E_i,\mathcal E_i)_{i\in I}$ be measurable spaces. A family
$(\mu_F)_{F\Subset I}$, indexed by all finite subsets of $I$, is a **consistent family of finite-dimensional
distributions** when each $\mu_F$ is a probability measure on
$\bigotimes_{i\in F}\mathcal E_i$, with the finite unordered product
sigma-algebra of [[def-coordinate-maps-and-cylinder-sigma-algebra]], and for
every pair of finite sets $F\subseteq G\subseteq I$ the pushforward of
$\mu_G$ under the restriction $p_{G,F}(x)=x|_F$ equals $\mu_F$; equivalently,
$\mu_G(p_{G,F}^{-1}(A))=\mu_F(A)$ for every
$A\in\bigotimes_{i\in F}\mathcal E_i$. The restriction is measurable since
inverse images of coordinate generators are coordinate generators. The empty
support carries the unique probability measure on the singleton empty product.

Reordering means choosing a different enumeration of the **same** finite set
$F$. If $e:[n]\to F$ is an enumeration, its displayed ordered law is the
pushforward of $\mu_F$ under $r_e(x)=(x_{e(0)},\ldots,x_{e(n-1)})$.
For another enumeration $e'$, the coordinate permutation $r_{e'}\circ r_e^{-1}$
pushes this ordered law to the one displayed using $e'$. This is automatic
from these definitions and does not require equal laws on different subsets
of $I$, or invariance under permutations of a fixed ordered product.
In particular, consistency is data about
every finite joint law, not merely the one-coordinate marginals.

The measurable space $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$ with its usual
topology is standard Borel.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For any set $I$, standard-Borel coordinate spaces $(E_i,\mathcal E_i)$, and consistent finite-dimensional laws $(\mu_F)_{F\Subset I}$, there is a unique probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathcal C_I$ whose $F$-coordinate marginal is $\mu_F$ for each finite $F$.

For measurable spaces $(E_i,\mathcal E_i)_{i\in I}$, put
$E=\prod_{i\in I}E_i$. For finite $F\subseteq I$, let
$\pi_F:E\to\prod_{i\in F}E_i$ be restriction to $F$ (the singleton empty
product when $F=\varnothing$). On $\prod_{i\in F}E_i$, write $q_i$ for the
$i$th coordinate map and define

$$\bigotimes_{i\in F}\mathcal E_i:=\sigma\{q_i^{-1}(A):i\in F,\ A\in\mathcal E_i\}.$$

For $F=\varnothing$ this is the two-set sigma-algebra on the singleton. If
$e:[n]\to F$ is any enumeration, coordinate relabelling identifies this
sigma-algebra with the recursively defined finite product sigma-algebra of
[[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]: both are
generated by the same coordinate inverse images. Thus the notation is
independent of the enumeration.

A **finite-coordinate cylinder** is $\pi_F^{-1}(A)$ for
$A\in\bigotimes_{i\in F}\mathcal E_i$. The **cylinder sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal C_I:=\sigma\{\pi_F^{-1}(A):F\subseteq I\text{ finite},\ A\in\bigotimes_{i\in F}\mathcal E_i\}.$$

This is the product sigma-algebra on the arbitrary product; the empty-support cylinder is either $\varnothing$ or $E$.

For $t\in I$, let $X_t:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(E_t,\mathcal E_t)$ be a random element. The family $X=(X_t)_{t\in I}$ is a **stochastic process**. For an ordered tuple of distinct times $(t_1,\ldots,t_n)$, its finite-dimensional distribution is the pushforward law of $(X_{t_1},\ldots,X_{t_n})$ on $\prod_{j<n}E_{t_{j+1}}$. These laws, including their coordinate order, form a consistent family under deletion and permutation of times.

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. A real stochastic process
$X=(X_t)_{t\in I}$ [[def-stochastic-process-and-finite-dimensional-distributions]]
is a **Gaussian process** if, for every integer $n\ge 1$, every time list
$t_1,\ldots,t_n\in I$, and every $a_1,\ldots,a_n\in\mathbb R$, the random
variable
$$
\sum_{j=1}^n a_jX_{t_j}
$$
has a normal law $N(m,\sigma^2)$ for some $m\in\mathbb R$ and
$\sigma\ge0$. Variance zero is allowed, so constant linear combinations are
included.

Equivalently, for every such time list the evaluation vector
$(X_{t_1},\ldots,X_{t_n})$ has a possibly singular multivariate normal law in
the sense of [[def-multivariate-normal-law]]. Indeed, that definition says
exactly that every scalar projection of the vector is normal. This also covers
repeated times, zero coefficients, and singular covariance matrices; no
distinct-time convention is needed for this definition.

Choice is declared because the library's scalar and multivariate normal-law
interfaces construct their probability laws and independent standard-normal
realizations under AC. The equivalence itself is only an unpacking of the
finite-dimensional projection definition and makes no further selection.

derivations.claim: For each nonempty finite $F\subseteq T$, use AC to choose an enumeration $e_F:\{1,\ldots,n\}\to F$. Set $a_i=m(e_F(i))$ and $\Sigma_{ij}=k(e_F(i),e_F(j))$. Positive semidefiniteness of $k$ makes $\Sigma$ positive semidefinite; [F1] supplies its positive square root and [F2] gives the possibly singular law $N_n(a,\Sigma)$. Push this law to $\mathbb R^F$ by relabelling coordinate $i$ as $e_F(i)$. A different enumeration changes both the mean and covariance by the same permutation; [F3] shows that the relabelled law is unchanged. For $F=\varnothing$, take the unique law on the singleton empty product.

If $F\subseteq G$ are finite, the characteristic function of the restriction pushforward of the $G$-law at $u\in\mathbb R^F$ is $ \exp\!\left(i\sum_{t\in F}u_t m(t)-\frac12\sum_{s,t\in F}u_su_t k(s,t)\right). $ This is also the characteristic function of the $F$-law. By [F3] the two pushforward laws agree, so the family constructed in step 1.1 is consistent in the sense of [F4]. The empty marginal is the singleton law.

Each coordinate space $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$ is standard Borel by [F5]. The consistent family from step 2.1 therefore satisfies [F6], which gives a unique probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathcal C_T$ with exactly these finite-coordinate marginals.

Define $X_t(x)=x(t)$ on $(\mathbb R^T,\mathcal C_T,\mu)$. By [F7] these coordinates are measurable, and step 3.1 gives each finite evaluation vector the stated multivariate normal law. Every finite linear combination is a scalar projection of such a vector, hence is normal by [F2]. Thus [F8] makes $X$ a Gaussian process. Its one- and two-coordinate laws give mean $m$ and covariance $k$, including zero-variance coordinates and singular finite covariance matrices.

The extension in step 3.1 is unique on $\mathcal C_T$. It supplies no topology or probability law on a path-continuous or Banach-valued function space, so no such regularity or tightness conclusion is included.

there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for

Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. A real stochastic process
$X=(X_t)_{t\in I}$ [[def-stochastic-process-and-finite-dimensional-distributions]]
is a **Gaussian process** if, for every integer $n\ge 1$, every time list
$t_1,\ldots,t_n\in I$, and every $a_1,\ldots,a_n\in\mathbb R$, the random
variable
$$

has a normal law $N(m,\sigma^2)$ for some $m\in\mathbb R$ and
$\sigma\ge0$. Variance zero is allowed, so constant linear combinations are

$(X_{t_1},\ldots,X_{t_n})$ has a possibly singular multivariate normal law in
the sense of [[def-multivariate-normal-law]]. Indeed, that definition says

interfaces construct their probability laws and independent standard-normal
realizations under AC. The equivalence itself is only an unpacking of the
finite-dimensional projection definition and makes no further selection.

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $m\ge1$ be finite, let $d_j\ge1$, and let
$Z_j$ for $1\le j\le m$ be mutually independent random elements of
$\mathbb R^{d_j}$. Suppose $Z_j\sim N_{d_j}(a_j,\Sigma_j)$, where each
$\Sigma_j$ is symmetric positive semidefinite. Put
$D=\sum_{j=1}^m d_j$, $Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m)$,
$a=(a_1,\ldots,a_m)$, and
$\Sigma=\operatorname{diag}(\Sigma_1,\ldots,\Sigma_m)$. Then
$$Z\sim N_D(a,\Sigma).$$
No covariance block needs to be invertible.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Assume AC. Let $X\in\mathbb R^d$ and $Y\in\mathbb R^m$, with $d,m\ge1$, be
jointly multivariate normal with mean $(a,b)$ and positive-semidefinite block
covariance
$$\Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}A&C\\C^T&B\end{pmatrix},$$
where $B$ is positive definite. Then
$$S=A-CB^{-1}C^T$$
is positive semidefinite, and for every $y\in\mathbb R^m$ the probability law
$$K(y,\cdot)=N_d\!\left(a+CB^{-1}(y-b),S\right)$$
is defined. The map $K$ is a probability kernel and is a conditional law of
$X$ given $Y$: for all Borel $E\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ and
$F\subseteq\mathbb R^m$,
$$\mathbb P(X\in E,Y\in F)=\int_F K(y,E)\,\mathbb P_Y(dy).$$
The covariance $A$ and the conditional covariance $S$ may be singular.
Positive definiteness of $B$ is required; no pseudoinverse formula for
singular $B$ is asserted.

Let $n\ge 1$ and let $A\in M_n(\mathbb C)$, with the real case obtained by
restricting scalars to $\mathbb R$. Then the following are equivalent:

1. $A$ has a Cholesky factorisation $A=LL^*$ with $L$ lower triangular and
   positive real diagonal.
2. $A$ is Hermitian positive definite.

When these conditions hold, the factor $L$ is unique.

Let $F$ be a field, let $n\ge 1$, and let $b\in F^n$.

If $L=(\ell_{ij})\in M_n(F)$ is lower triangular with every diagonal entry
$\ell_{ii}\ne 0$, the **forward substitution solve** of $Lx=b$ is the recursive
construction

$$x_i:=\frac{1}{\ell_{ii}}\left(b_i-\sum_{j<i}\ell_{ij}x_j\right)\qquad(0\le i<n).$$If $U=(u_{ij})\in M_n(F)$ is upper triangular with every diagonal entry $u_{ii}\ne 0$, the **backward substitution solve** of $Ux=b$ is the recursive construction$$x_i:=\frac{1}{u_{ii}}\left(b_i-\sum_{j>i}u_{ij}x_j\right)\qquad(n-1\ge i\ge 0).$$

The triangular vocabulary is from
[[def-triangular-and-diagonal-matrices-over-a-commutative-ring]]. The matrix
product convention from [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]] is the one
used when later items rewrite these recursions as matrix equations.

Let $F$ be a field, let $n\ge 1$, and let $b\in F^n$.

1. If $L\in M_n(F)$ is lower triangular with nonzero diagonal, the forward
   substitution recursion of
   [[def-forward-and-back-substitution-for-triangular-systems]] produces the
   unique solution of $Lx=b$.
2. If $U\in M_n(F)$ is upper triangular with nonzero diagonal, the backward
   substitution recursion produces the unique solution of $Ux=b$.

Each solve uses exactly $n$ divisions,
$\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$ multiplications, and $\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$ additions or
subtractions, hence $O(n^2)$ scalar operations.

derivations.claim: By [F1], the concatenated finite evaluation vector $U=(f_{X_*},f_X)$ is multivariate normal with mean $(m_*,m_X)$ and covariance $ \begin{pmatrix}K_{**}&K_{*X}\\K_{X*}&K_{XX}\end{pmatrix}. $ This remains valid when either list has repetitions.

The vector $\epsilon$ is multivariate normal with mean zero and covariance $R$. Each coordinate of $U$ is a measurable function of the process coordinates, so $\sigma(U)\subseteq\sigma(f)$. By [F2] and the independence hypothesis, $\sigma(\epsilon)$ is independent of $\sigma(f)$ and hence of $\sigma(U)$. Applying [F3] to $U$ and $\epsilon$ shows that $Z=(f_{X_*},f_X,\epsilon)$ is jointly multivariate normal with block-diagonal covariance between $U$ and $\epsilon$.

Apply the linear map $(u,v,e)\mapsto(u,v+e)$ to $Z$. Every scalar projection of the result is a scalar projection of $Z$, hence is normal by [F4]; its mean is $(m_*,m_X)$. The Gaussian vectors have finite second moments, so independence and $E\epsilon=0$ give $\operatorname{Cov}(f_{X_*},\epsilon)=0$ and $\operatorname{Cov}(Y)=K_{XX}+R=C$. By step 1.1, $\operatorname{Cov}(f_{X_*},f_X)=K_{*X}$, so $(f_{X_*},Y)$ is jointly Gaussian with covariance $ \begin{pmatrix}K_{**}&K_{*X}\\K_{X*}&C\end{pmatrix}. $

Apply [F5] with $A=K_{**}$, cross-covariance $K_{*X}$, and observed covariance $B=C\succ0$. The result is a probability-kernel version for every $y$, with the displayed mean and Schur-complement covariance; [F5] also proves this covariance is positive semidefinite even if singular.

If $\eta_*$ is present, it is jointly independent of the process and $\epsilon$ by hypothesis. By [F3], the stack $(f_{X_*},f_X,\epsilon,\eta_*)$ is jointly Gaussian. The linear map $(u,v,e,h)\mapsto(u+h,v+e)$ has mean $(m_*,m_X)$, cross-covariance $K_{*X}$, observed covariance $C$, and prediction covariance $K_{**}+R_*$. Applying [F5] to this pair gives the stated noisy-prediction law.

By [F6], write $C=LL^T$. For any right-hand side $b$, solve $Lz=b$ by forward substitution and $L^Tu=z$ by backward substitution; [F8] gives both unique solutions. Then $Cu=L(L^Tu)=Lz=b$, so $u=C^{-1}b$. Applying this to $b=y-m_X$ and, column by column, to $K_{X*}$ evaluates both formula terms without forming the inverse.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a set, let $m:T\to\mathbb R$, and let
$k:T\times T\to\mathbb R$ be symmetric and positive semidefinite, meaning that
for every finite list $t_1,\ldots,t_n\in T$ and every $a\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$
\sum_{i,j=1}^n a_i a_j k(t_i,t_j)\ge0.
$$
There is a unique probability measure $\mu$ on the cylinder sigma-algebra
$\mathcal C_T$ of $\mathbb R^T$ whose marginal on each finite-coordinate space
$\mathbb R^F$, for $F\subseteq T$ finite, is the Gaussian law with mean
$(m(t))_{t\in F}$ and covariance matrix $(k(s,t))_{s,t\in F}$. The coordinate
process $X_t(x)=x(t)$ is Gaussian, has mean function $m$, and has covariance
kernel $k$. This construction gives only the cylinder-space process; it
asserts no sample-path continuity, joint measurability in $(t,x)$, or tight

derivations.claim: For any finite coefficient list, the constant kernel's quadratic form is $(\sum_i a_i)^2\ge0$. Thus [F1] constructs the cylinder GP and [F2] supplies $N_2(0,I_2)$. Their product probability exists by [F3]; its process and noise random elements are measurable by [F5] and independent by [F4].

Hence it is positive definite and $C^{-1}=\frac13\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\-1&2\end{pmatrix}$. For the repeated test list, $K_{*X}=K_{**}=J_2$. Since $C$ is positive definite, the hypotheses of [F6] hold.

The prior observation covariance and conditional predictive covariance are both singular, whereas the matrix inverted by the formula is the positive-definite observed covariance $C$. This verifies why singular prior and predictive blocks are permitted under the stated condition.

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

Assume AC and let $f=(f_t)_{t\in T}$ be a real Gaussian process with mean
$m$ and covariance kernel $k$; when $m$ and $k$ are specified as a prior,
the canonical cylinder-space process exists by
[[thm-gaussian-process-exists-from-mean-and-positive-semidefinite-covariance-kernel]].
Let $X=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in T^n$ and $X_*=(x_1^*,\ldots,x_p^*)\in T^p$,
where $n,p\ge1$ and repeated indices are allowed. Write
$f_X=(f_{x_i})_{i=1}^n$, $f_{X_*}=(f_{x_j^*})_{j=1}^p$,
$m_X=(m(x_i))_{i=1}^n$, and $m_*=(m(x_j^*))_{j=1}^p$. For finite lists
$A=(a_i)$ and $B=(b_j)$, define
$K_{AB}=(k(a_i,b_j))_{i,j}$.

Let $\epsilon\sim N_n(0,R)$ be independent of the process, where $R$ is
symmetric positive semidefinite, and set $Y=f_X+\epsilon$. Assume the
observed covariance $C=K_{XX}+R$ is positive definite. Then a version of the
conditional law of $f_{X_*}$ given $Y=y$ is, for every $y\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$
N_p\!\left(m_*+K_{*X}C^{-1}(y-m_X),\;K_{**}-K_{*X}C^{-1}K_{X*}\right).
$$
The displayed conditional covariance is positive semidefinite and may be
singular; $K_{XX}$ and $K_{**}$ may also be singular. If a prediction-noise
vector $\eta_*\sim N_p(0,R_*)$ jointly independent of the process and
$\epsilon$ is added to $f_{X_*}$, with $R_*$ symmetric positive semidefinite,
the conditional mean is unchanged and
$R_*$ is added to the conditional covariance. The displayed kernel is a
version defined at every $y$; conditional-law versions are determined only
$P_Y$-almost surely.

For computation, the occurrences of $C^{-1}v$ mean solving $Cu=v$. Since
$C$ is positive definite, its Cholesky factorization and forward/back
substitution evaluate these solves without forming $C^{-1}$.

derivations.claim: For any finite list of indices, group coefficients at repeated sites. The equality kernel's quadratic form is the sum, over distinct sites $t$, of $(\sum_{i:t_i=t}a_i)^2$, hence is nonnegative. By [F1] the canonical GP law exists and [F2] supplies the $N(0,1)$ noise law. Their product probability exists by [F3]; its process and noise random elements are measurable by [F5] and independent by [F4].
Here $K_{XX}=1$, $K_{**}=1$, $K_{*X}=K_{X*}=0$, and the noise covariance is $R=1$. Thus $C=K_{XX}+R=2>0$, so [F6] applies.

The formula in [F6] gives posterior mean $0+0\cdot 2^{-1}(y-0)=0$ and variance $1-0\cdot2^{-1}\cdot0=1$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$. Hence the posterior version at the unobserved independent index is its original $N(0,1)$ law.
